output:
*Interview with Mademoiselle Lina Ruedi, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Mademoiselle Ruedi, thank you for waiting. I know it is late and you have been up. Please sit down.

MLLE RUEDI: I will stand, if it is the same to you. I have been sitting all day.

MATTHEY: As you like. Tell me about the dinner, in your own order.

MLLE RUEDI: When the temple struck nine, the master made us all show our watches. He does it every year. Mine was exact. I regulated it myself, so I knew it would be. The doctor's was two minutes ahead. Monsieur Girard would not take his out of his pocket at all, and the master remarked on it.

MATTHEY: Did you go back to the atelier after dinner?

MLLE RUEDI: Yes. I worked beside the master.

MATTHEY: Tell me about the clocks while you worked.

MLLE RUEDI: The hall clock downstairs struck ten when the regulator showed twelve minutes to ten. The master said what he always says about that clock. It is an old joke between him and the clock, and I do not think it has anything to do with this. Then the temple struck ten, and the regulator agreed with the bell exactly. I noticed that, because the master was particular about it.

MATTHEY: Take your time. What happened next?

MLLE RUEDI: He sent me downstairs when the regulator showed twenty past ten. I want to be exact about that. The regulator was running then, and he was well. I went straight down to the kitchen.

MATTHEY: How many years have you worked for him?

MLLE RUEDI: Since I was seventeen. He was the most exact man I have ever known. He could not abide a watch that lied about the hour, and he could not abide a person who did.

MATTHEY: Was there anything in the atelier that you noticed, apart from the regulator?

MLLE RUEDI: The repeater, Monsieur. He spent four years on it. When you press the slide it speaks. The low notes are the hours. Each quarter is a doubled note, and the minutes past the quarter are high notes, quick and light. He wanted it to strike the first minute of the new century. I helped with the hairsprings, and I know what that cost him.

MATTHEY: Did you see him at all that afternoon?

MLLE RUEDI: Yes. I saw the master in the kitchen with Rosa's clock in his hands. He was laughing.

MATTHEY: Did you ask him why?

MLLE RUEDI: No, Monsieur. I did not ask.

MATTHEY: Then tell me about the kitchen, after you went down.

MLLE RUEDI: I stayed in the kitchen with Rosa. I looked at Rosa's kitchen clock when Madame's piano began. It showed two minutes to eleven. When the piano stopped, Rosa's kitchen clock showed eleven minutes past eleven.

MATTHEY: You were watching the clock closely.

MLLE RUEDI: One watches a clock when one is waiting, Monsieur. I was waiting for something, though I did not know what.

MATTHEY: And you remained in the kitchen until?

MLLE RUEDI: Until after the temple struck eleven.

MATTHEY: Is there anything about the regulator, or the master's watches, that you think I should understand?

MLLE RUEDI: I do not speculate. I tell you what I saw and what I heard. I would not put a theory into a clock, and I will not put one into your notebook.

MATTHEY: That is fair. Is there anything else you think I should know?

MLLE RUEDI: Only that my own watch is exact, and that the master would have wanted you to know it. He was not a man who forgave a careless account of the time.
